study.title: Joshua 5 Renewal of the covenant, Passover, and the holy presence of God
study.overview: Joshua 5 shows that entry into Canaan does not begin with a military strategy, but with the restoration of the covenant and with acts of worship. The chapter alternates between the fear of enemies, the obedience of Israel to circumcision, the celebration of the Passover, the end of the manna, and the appearance of the Prince of the army of the LORD. The central point is that the conquest of the earth depends, first of all, on holiness, on the fidelity of God and Joshua's submission to divine authority.

outline.title: The fear of the Canaanites and the obedience to circumcision
outline.explanation: The crossing of the Jordan makes the hearts of the peoples of Canaan fade. Before advancing against Jericho, the LORD sends Joshua to renew circumcision, and he obeys with instruments of stone, marking the people for the covenant.

outline.title: Why the new generation needed to be circumcised
outline.explanation: The text explains that the men of the generation of the exodus died in the desert because of disobedience, while the children born on the way had not been circumcised. After the rite, the people remain in the camp until heals, showing that obedience also requires waiting and vulnerability.

outline.title: Gilgal, the Passover and the end of the manna
outline.explanation: God declares that he took the humiliation out of Egypt, and the place is called Gilgal. Then Israel celebrates the Passover and eats the fruit of the earth. The manna ceases because the miraculous provision gives way to the ordinary provision of Canaan.

outline.title: The Apparition of the Prince of the Army of the LORD
outline.explanation: At the next to Jericho, Joshua finds an armed man who is revealed as Prince of the LORD's army. The answer is not to choose human sides, but to recognize the sanctity of the place. Joshua prostrates and receives order to take off the sandals, a sign of reverence before the holy presence of God.

study.context: The chapter takes place shortly after the crossing of the Jordan and before the attack on Jericho. The notes provided highlight that the shock of the miraculous crossing alarmed the Canaanites and that Israel was at the gates of conquest. They also indicate that circumcision and Easter function as renewal of the alliance exactly at the beginning of the campaign. The text no longer provides secure historical details moreover, and any magnification beyond this information should not be treated as sure.
study.theology: Joshua 5 teaches that victory in Canaan begins with repentance, consecration, and memory of redemption. Circumcision points to belonging to the covenant and to the need for personal participation in it; the Passover recalls the deliverance worked by God; the cessation manna shows that divine care continues, but in a new way, when the people enter the promised land. The view of the Prince of the LORD's army corrects any idea that God is simply at the service of Israel: the true focus is the holiness of God and the submission of the human leader to his presence. In Protestant evangelical perspective, the chapter can be read as a call to obedient faith: God leads his people, but requires reverence, purification, and confidence in his direction before any external advancement.

scholarViews.insight: The impossible crossing of the Jordan left the Canaanites terrified, because they realized that they faced a people whose God is more powerful than their gods.
Joshua begins the campaign with acts of devotion; the divine apparition comes after the circumcision and the Passover, suggesting that God is known in the way of obedience.
The order to remove the sandals indicates that the place is holy and recalls the scene of the burning bush, suggesting a divine manifestation similar to that given to Moses.

questions: What does Joshua 5 reveal about the right order between worship and practical action in the life of God's people?
How does circumcision, the Passover and the end of the manna show that God is forming a dependent people of him, and not just an army?
How does the holiness of God's presence correct our tendency to treat him as someone in the service of our plans?
study.practice: Before facing important decisions, take a time to renew your obedience to God in prayer, confession and listening to the Word. Reflect if there are areas in which you are moving in haste, but without reverence. It is also worth remembering, by the Passover and the manna, that God has already sustained his people in the past and continues to sustain in a faithful way, albeit by means different from those you expected. If you lead someone, learn from Joshua: spiritual authority begins with submission to the presence of God.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not accurately clarify who is the Prince of the army of the LORD in terms of theological identity, so this must be treated with caution. It is also not possible to safely affirm, only with the notes provided, additional details about geography, the exact duration of recovery after circumcision or the wide chronology of the achievement. The expression "second time" in verse 2 is interpretative in the text itself and should not be magnified beyond the meaning provided here.
